title: AI models flub these intelligence tests. Can you fare any better?
gist: Puzzle benchmarks show frontier AI models rapidly saturating some tests (NYT Connections went from 18% solved to near-perfect within months) while still failing badly at 3D spatial reasoning, complexity-scaled logic puzzles, and genuine (versus memorized) reasoning -- evidence that headline benchmark gains can overstate general reasoning ability.

themes.theme: Puzzles as a long-running AI capability barometer

insights.claim: Puzzles and games have been used to benchmark AI progress since 1959, when IBM scientist Arthur Samuel's checkers-playing algorithm popularized the term 'machine learning'; chess, Go, and today's Connections/ARC-AGI/SimpleBench suites continue that same tradition of using games as a proxy for measuring frontier AI capability.
insights.speaker: Grace Huckins
insights.so_what: Puzzle-based benchmarks have a 65-year track record as an AI capability proxy, but that history also shows benchmarks get 'solved' and retired repeatedly -- a reason to treat any single current benchmark's headline score as temporary, not a durable moat signal.
insights.quote: The term “machine learning” was popularized in a 1959 article by the IBM computer scientist Arthur Samuel about an algorithm that learned to play checkers.
insights.locator: Puzzles and games have been central

insights.claim: In late 2024 a Columbia University team found that even the best AI models could solve only 18% of New York Times Connections puzzles, but by early 2025 some models could solve them near-perfectly every time -- a benchmark going from largely unsolved to essentially saturated within a few months.
insights.speaker: Grace Huckins
insights.so_what: Illustrates how fast a specific 'hard for AI' benchmark can saturate once labs target it -- a caution against reading any single frozen benchmark gap as a durable competitive moat for either model builders or evaluators.
insights.quote: even the best models could figure out only 18% of the infamous New York Times Connections puzzles
insights.locator: Judged purely on its puzzling skills

themes.theme: Spatial and visual reasoning remains a weak spot

insights.claim: Despite having the ability to analyze visual inputs, today's language models still fail badly at mental-rotation puzzles that ask whether two images depict the same 3D object from different angles -- a domain where humans, especially spatial thinkers like architects and engineers, have a clear advantage.
insights.speaker: Grace Huckins
insights.so_what: A specific, persistent capability gap -- true 3D object manipulation, not just image description -- relevant to how much weight to put on current multimodal models for physical-world and robotics applications.
insights.quote: they still fail abysmally at these puzzles.
insights.locator: Let’s start with a domain where humans

insights.claim: On the ARC-AGI benchmark, models perform meaningfully better when a puzzle grid is given as a string of numbers encoding each cell's color rather than as an image, and research shows that even when models answer ARC-AGI questions correctly, they often rely on convoluted, non-generalizable rules rather than the simple visual concepts humans use to solve the same puzzles.
insights.speaker: Grace Huckins
insights.so_what: Suggests some ARC-AGI score gains reflect better numeric/textual pattern-matching rather than genuine abstract visual reasoning -- a reason to discount headline benchmark improvements when the underlying solution method doesn't generalize the way human reasoning does.
insights.locator: AI doesn’t just bungle visual problems in 3D

insights.claim: A 2024 study by researchers from Google and the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign found that when a Knights-and-Knaves logic puzzle is only slightly varied from forms a model likely saw in training, the model tends to 'whiz by' the key differences and answer with the memorized pattern rather than actually re-reasoning through the new version.
insights.speaker: Grace Huckins
insights.so_what: Indicates strong benchmark performance can reflect training-data pattern recall rather than robust reasoning -- an important caveat when using logic-puzzle benchmark scores as evidence for a model's general reasoning capability claims.
insights.quote: When a puzzle closely resembles one a model saw during training, the model may whiz by key differences and respond with what it memorized.

insights.claim: SimpleBench questions are designed to closely resemble more complicated problems models likely encountered in training, and even top-tier models trip on them, while humans easily spot the trick -- reinforcing that benchmark difficulty for AI does not track benchmark difficulty for humans.
insights.speaker: Grace Huckins
insights.so_what: A concrete example of a benchmark specifically constructed to expose the memorization-versus-reasoning gap -- useful for evaluators to distinguish genuine reasoning improvement from surface pattern matching in vendor benchmark claims.
insights.quote: Humans spot the trick, but even top-tier models trip.
insights.locator: The same principle may be at work

insights.claim: Apple researchers found that LLMs can ace simple versions of the Tower of Hanoi and river-crossing puzzles, but as the number of disks or people involved hits six or higher, the models begin to falter -- though commentators questioned whether this reveals a unique LLM reasoning limitation or simply reflects that errors naturally increase as problem complexity rises.
insights.speaker: Grace Huckins
insights.so_what: A widely cited ('went viral') but contested finding about LLM reasoning scaling limits -- worth tracking as a live debate rather than settled evidence when assessing claims about LLM reasoning ceilings.
insights.quote: As the number of disks or people hits six and higher, the models began to falter.
insights.locator: One study from researchers at Apple

insights.claim: Researchers from the University of Washington, Stanford University, and the Allen Institute for AI found that LLMs struggle similarly with logic-grid puzzles that require deducing multiple individuals' attributes from a list of clues, reinforcing that structured, multi-step constraint-satisfaction reasoning remains a weak spot even as single-step benchmark scores improve.
insights.speaker: Grace Huckins
insights.so_what: Adds a second, independent research group's evidence of the same complexity-scaling weakness seen in the Apple study, strengthening the case that multi-step constraint reasoning is a durable (not one-off) LLM limitation worth discounting into any 'reasoning model' capability claim.

themes.theme: Human and machine cognition fail differently

insights.claim: Psychologists have designed problem sets that invert the usual pattern: on certain intuitive-math trick questions, humans tend to give fast, wrong 'knee-jerk' answers, whereas AI models respond more deliberatively and get them right -- showing machine and human cognitive failure modes are not simply 'AI is worse at everything,' but genuinely different in kind.
insights.speaker: Grace Huckins
insights.so_what: A reminder that AI capability comparisons are not one-dimensional -- some benchmarks designed to catch AI weaknesses instead reveal human cognitive biases that AI models don't share, which matters for how 'AI versus human' capability claims get framed.
insights.quote: humans often give knee-jerk answers, whereas models will respond deliberatively.
